teaser: In 1863, Parisians lined up in front of this picnic to laugh at it.

lesson.text: Paris, spring 1863. In a side gallery, visitors press around a large canvas, and they are laughing. People nudge each other and call their friends over. Within days the newspapers are full of jokes about the picture, and of outrage too.

The gallery had a nickname: the Salon des Refusés, the “show of the rejected”. That year the jury of the official Salon, the state exhibition that could make or break a career, turned away so many works that Emperor Napoleon III let the losers hang next door. Édouard Manet, 31, was one of them.

Nudity was not the problem. The official Salon was full of bare skin that same year, and nobody blinked, because those bodies belonged to Venus or to nymphs in some faraway myth. Manet changed three or four things. They were enough.

lesson.title: What the crowd saw
lesson.text: Four details that turned a picnic into a scandal.

spots.title: Her eyes
spots.text: She turns her head and looks straight at you, chin on her hand, calm and a little amused. Painted goddesses looked away. She has noticed you staring.

spots.title: Her clothes
spots.text: A blue dress, a straw hat with a ribbon, lying in a heap beside the spilled basket. A goddess is naked by nature. This woman got undressed.

spots.title: A necktie
spots.text: The man beside her wears a dark jacket, white collar and tie: the outfit of a Parisian in 1863. No toga, no legend to hide behind.

spots.title: The bather
spots.text: A second woman wades in her shift. She seems far away, yet she is nearly as big as the people in front, as if cut out and pasted in.

lesson.text: The woman in front had a name. Victorine Meurent, a model of about 18 with red hair, posed for Manet in his studio, not in a forest. The two men are thought to be one of his brothers and his future brother-in-law. They chat. Nobody looks at anybody.
Victorine Meurent became a painter in her own right. In 1876 the Salon jury accepted her work in the same year it refused Manet's.

Here is the part the laughing crowd missed. The trio is copied, pose for pose, from a print after Raphael, the most respected painter of the Renaissance, showing river gods sitting on a bank. And clothed men with naked women in a landscape hung a short walk away in the Louvre, in a famous Venetian picture.
Manet did not attack the old masters. He replayed one of their scenes with people from his own time, and the result showed how much the “noble nude” depended on costume and distance.

The handling shocked painters as much as the subject shocked the public. Academic teaching asked for modeling, the slow shading that makes a body look round. Manet lights Victorine like a flash: pale skin, almost no half-tones, set flat against dark coats. The woods behind are brushed in like a theater backdrop.
The canvas measures about 2.08 by 2.65 meters (roughly 7 by 9 feet). That size was normally kept for battles, saints and kings. Manet's first title for it was simply “Le Bain”, the bath.
In all that loose green, Manet slipped in one small living thing. It has nothing to do with the picnic, and most visitors walk past without seeing it. Look high, above everyone's heads.
Something is flying in this painting. Can you spot it?

spots.title: A bird in mid-air
spots.text: A small bird with an orange breast, usually called a bullfinch, hangs at the very top with wings spread. Three or four strokes of the brush, no more.

lesson.text: Compare that quick bird with the cherries, the bread and the silver flask at the bottom left, painted with real care. Manet finishes what interests him and sketches the rest. To critics of 1863 this looked lazy. To younger painters it looked like permission.

Two years later a 24-year-old named Claude Monet began his own, even larger “Déjeuner sur l'herbe”, this time painted with real outdoor light. And the idea of showing outside the official Salon stuck: in 1874, Monet and his friends held the first independent exhibition of the group soon called the Impressionists.
Almost a century on, Pablo Picasso became obsessed with this picture. Between 1959 and 1962 he made 27 paintings and well over a hundred drawings reworking its four figures.

The crowd of 1863 is gone, but the painting still does the same thing to whoever stands before it. Three people ignore one another, and the fourth looks out at the one person who was not invited. What does she expect you to say?

quiz.question: What was the Salon des Refusés?
options: An exhibition of works the official jury had rejected
quiz.explanation: Napoleon III allowed rejected artists to show their works next to the official Salon in 1863.

quiz.question: Why did this nude shock when Salon nudes did not?
options: She is a modern woman, not a goddess, and she looks at the viewer
She is painted larger than life
She is shown in a church
quiz.explanation: Her discarded clothes, the men's modern suits and her direct gaze removed the excuse of myth.

quiz.question: Where did Manet borrow the poses of the three seated figures?
quiz.explanation: The trio repeats river gods from a print after Raphael.

quiz.question: What is “modeling” in painting?
options: Gradual shading that makes a form look round
quiz.explanation: Modeling is the slow shading that gives volume, which Manet largely skipped.

quiz.question: Which animal hides at the top of the canvas?
quiz.explanation: A small bird with an orange breast flies among the leaves at the very top.

facts.text: Manet painted the scene outdoors, in a forest near Paris.
facts.explanation: Victorine Meurent posed in his studio; the woods are brushed in like a backdrop.

facts.text: The model, Victorine Meurent, later showed her own paintings at the Salon.
facts.explanation: In 1876 the jury accepted her work and refused Manet's.

facts.text: The painting's first title was “Le Bain”, the bath.
facts.explanation: Manet first showed it under that title in 1863.
